processing: The pale stems and petioles sorted from gyokuro and high-grade sencha during refining in Kyushu, lightly fired; the same product that Kyoto calls karigane, and the upper end of what Japan generally calls kukicha.
harvest_season: First-flush by-product (April–May); 'gyokuro shiraore' comes only from the spring gyokuro refining.
appearance_dry: Pale, whitish-green stems and petioles with a few dark needles mixed in; the name's characters read 'white' and 'fold', after the light-coloured stems.
appearance_wet: Soft pale green stems and a few leaf pieces.
taste_profile: Light, sweet, with a gentle umami and a cool, refreshing finish, often with a faint vanilla-like creaminess in gyokuro lots.

brewing.notes: Cooler water and a slightly longer first steep for gyokuro shiraore; plain shiraore from sencha can take 80 °C. The stems are light and bulky, so weigh them. Cold-brews well.

vintage_note: Sold by Kyushu shops as a by-product of the current year's spring refining, labelled with the parent tea (gyokuro shiraore being the better grade) and sometimes the district (Yame); it is at its best in early summer and should be finished within the year, sealed and cold. No ageing tradition.
description:
Shiraore is Kyushu's name for stem tea, the pale stalks and petioles sorted out of gyokuro and good sencha during refining, made in Yame, Kagoshima and Saga. The characters read 'white' and 'fold' or 'break', after the whitish stems, and the product is the same thing Kyoto calls karigane, the better end of what the rest of the country calls kukicha.

The best of it is gyokuro shiraore from Yame, the stems of shaded tea: because the bush was covered for three weeks before picking, the stems carry the same amino-acid sweetness as the leaf, with far less caffeine and almost no astringency. Plain shiraore from sencha is lighter and more grassy. Both are lightly fired after sorting and sold in spring and early summer, when the first-flush refining is done.

Brew gyokuro shiraore cool, 6 g for 150 ml at 65–70 °C for a little over a minute, and it gives a pale, clear cup that is sweet, softly savoury and refreshing, often with a faint vanilla-like creaminess; sencha shiraore can take 80 °C and makes a clean, everyday tea. The stems are light and bulky, so weigh them, and give the first steep time; it cold-brews well and is a good evening tea.

Yame shops sell it labelled gyokuro shiraore or simply shiraore, with the district and sometimes the parent tea's grade, at a price well below gyokuro; look for pale green stems rather than brown woody ones. It is a current-year by-product that is best in the first months and should be finished within the year, sealed and cold.

If you like it, move up to the parent Yame gyokuro, or sideways to a Kyoto karigane and see whether you can tell the difference.
history:
Shiraore is the name used in Kyushu for stem tea from gyokuro and good sencha, the regional counterpart of Kyoto's karigane. It belongs to the by-products of refining and owes its appeal to the high theanine in the stems.

Little is documented about when the name came into use or who first sold it. The usual reading links it to the pale colour of the stems, though that is more explanation than record. The word is sometimes used simply as another name for kukicha, so it is worth checking what the parent tea was.
